## 8. `nat`: a size in a type

### What the specification says it is

A `nat` static parameter is the keyword `nat` followed by an identifier, in the
same white brackets as a type parameter
(`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:68-81`). Three sentences fix its
meaning. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values"
(`:82`) — so a size is not erased. A `nat` parameter "may be used to
instantiate other `nat` parameters, or to appear in any context that a variable
of type `N32` can appear, except that it cannot be assigned to" (`:83-86`) — so
in value position it is a read-only number, and in type position it may only
instantiate other sizes. And the chapter's single example is exactly an array
shape: `makeVector[\T extends Number, nat s0\](): Vector[\T,s0\]`
(`:94-97`), one symbol occurring in the parameter list and in the return type,
which must agree.

The chapter opens with its own status note: "Non-type static parameters and
static expressions are not yet supported. The examples in this chapter are not
tested nor run by the interpreter." (`:15-17`). So the gap is not a regression;
the team shipped the specification saying so (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a).

Sizes were meant to check shapes, not to optimize anything: the spec builds no
optimization on them anywhere (FACTS, execution model). The one recorded
implementation stance in the team's own internal appendix is "don't
instantiate" — the checker treats a size as opaque, two different literals are
different types, and arithmetic on sizes is not something the checker reasons
about (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a, from
`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex:182, 206`).

### Where sizes actually occur

The interpreter's library has 81 declarations with `nat`/`int`/`bool`
parameters; the target program's array vocabularies have 30 and 27; the
compiler's own prelude has exactly **one**, and it is empty:
`trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\] extends Object end`
(`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:512`; census in `nat-checking-plan.md` §d). In
every one of them the arguments are symbols and literals; the census found no
arithmetic inside white brackets in the library or either vocabulary
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §d) — with three exceptions in storing objects that a
later review found (`array-design-review.md` finding 5), which matters if the
rule adopted is "refuse arithmetic".

That the compiler prelude has one empty `nat` declaration is the shape of the
whole problem: the compiler's library is written to stay inside what the
checker can do (`spec-to-implementation.md` §4.3; FACTS, ledger 307).

### What the checker lacks, in three parts

**Representation.** There is no inference variable for a size. When the checker
needs to infer static arguments at a call, it makes one fresh variable per
static parameter; for a type parameter that is `TypeArg(_InferenceVarType)` and
for an operator parameter `OpArg(_InferenceVarOp)`, and for `KindNat`,
`KindInt`, `KindBool`, `KindDim` and `KindUnit` it is `NI.nyi()`
(`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:546-559`). That call is reached from
ordinary call-site inference and from the overloading checker alike, which is
why the crash appears twice when a library is checked
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §b). Two representations are on the table: a new AST
node `_InferenceVarInt` beside the existing two, which is symmetric but
regenerates every visitor class; or an `IntRef` with a reserved name, which
needs no AST change and can therefore be prototyped under a classpath shadow
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, "Representation").

**Equality.** Two sizes are compared in exactly one place, and today it says
yes to everything: `case (_: IntArg, _: IntArg) => pTrue()`, under the comment
"Not handling all static args properly yet"
(`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:332`). Exclusion has the twin hole
(`:445-451`), and the export checker's `equalIntExprs` is `= false`
(`typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:648`). The rule the plan proposes is the
interpreter's own: a literal must equal a literal, a symbol equals itself, a
symbol is not a literal, and an inference variable takes an equality constraint
— which is a port of `IntNat.unifyStaticArg`
(`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:127-147`;
`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, "Rules").

**Inference.** The constraint solver has two tracks, types and operators: `And`
carries a map per type variable and a map per operator variable
(`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:50`), and `solve` returns a pair of
substitutions (`:420-460`). A size needs a third track, unified as the operator
track is, by cliques with structural equality
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, §"What it touches"). One more hole travels with it:
`hasInferenceVars` looks only for type variables
(`STypesUtil.scala:778-789`), so an unsolved size would leak silently into a
generated name instead of producing "not enough context".

**Size of the change, and the caveat on it.** About 24 functions in five Scala
files, 200-300 lines, most of it the mechanical third track in `Formula.scala`;
no catalogued test flips; five compiler tests must stay green
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §d). The caveat: the plan's "no Java" is unproven — one
of the two known crashes has Java frames, in the static-type replacer, and six
Java files in `compiler/` handle `IntArg`
(`array-design-review.md` finding 6). The instrument that settles it is a
shadow session (edited copies compiled and put first on the class path), which
has been done once before for a checker plan and gated green
(FACTS, the template-checking fix), and has not been done for this one
(`array-design-review.md` §1b).

### What the loader and the code generator lack

Section 6 in one paragraph: the size is mangled into the instantiation name
(`NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`) and nothing reads it back — the
runtime consults only the operator kind (`Naming.java:95-108`), the generic
RTTI class has no size field (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`), a
size in an `extends` clause is refused outright
(`CodeGen.java:5793`), and a size in value position compiles to a reference the
loader cannot satisfy (`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). So the first
sized object that compiles will need work in Java after the checker work in
Scala; the review counts at least three gated batches where the design counted
two (`array-design-review.md` finding 6).

### The thing a `nat` fix does not fix

The target program's values carry their sizes at run time and not in their
static types: `array[\E\](n)` reflects `n` into a size and returns the *unsized*
`Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, and the interpreter then dispatches on the run-time
object. On the compile path the static type is what is consulted, so the
applications fail even with no `nat` in sight — probe `p3_static_dispatch`
above (`array-design-review.md` finding 1). Teaching the checker sizes makes
sized *declarations* checkable; making the model's *applications* check is a
separate decision about how the model is typed.

### Four precedents, and what each would mean here

These four are background from outside this tree — nothing in the repository
documents them — offered because each one already took a decision that is now
in front of us. The in-tree consequence after each is cited.

**Dependent ML.** Xi and Pfenning's design indexes types by a separate, decidable
domain of integers, with constraints solved by an arithmetic solver, precisely
so that dependent types do not drag full term evaluation into type checking.
Here it names the boundary question: whether sizes live in a small language of
their own with a solver behind them, or stay symbols and literals compared by
equality — which is what the plan proposes and what the team's own "don't
instantiate" stance implies (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a, §c).

**X10's constrained types.** X10 attaches boolean constraints to types —
`Array[T]{rank==2}` — and discharges them with a pluggable constraint solver,
which buys array-shape checking at the cost of a solver in the compiler and a
constraint language in the surface syntax. Here it is the shape of the *next*
step past equality, and the reason to take equality first: Fortress already has
the syntax for it, a where clause with an `IntConstraint`
(`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast:1485-1496`), and the checker ignores
where clauses entirely (`STypesUtil.scala:625`;
`typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:126`).

**Haskell's type-level naturals.** `GHC.TypeLits` gives a kind of naturals with
literals and type-level arithmetic that the compiler solves only for closed
literals — real algebra needs a normalizing solver supplied as a plugin — plus
a `KnownNat` dictionary to read a size back as a value. Here the second half
already exists (`LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi` reflects a size to a number),
and the first half is the honest price of arithmetic in types, which is why the
plan draws its line at symbols and literals and refuses `Vector[\T, n+1\]` as
ill-formed rather than promising to check it (`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, §g).

**C++ non-type template parameters.** `template<size_t N>` instantiates a
distinct class per value, equality of sizes is syntactic identity after
constant folding, and the size is a compile-time constant with no run-time
representation at all. Here it is the contrast that matters most: Fortress
sizes are "instantiated at runtime with numeric values"
(`trait-parameters.tex:82`), the interpreter really does evaluate `+`, `-` and
`*` on them while instantiating
(`interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:431-464`), and the class loader stamps by
name only (section 6) — so C++'s per-value specialization is *not* what this
loader does, and any plan that assumes a size disappears at compile time is
assuming the wrong runtime.

### What is a decision, not a fact

Four things the record leaves to Pavol, each already stated in a report:
whether the inference variable is a new AST node or a reserved name
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c); what an unconstrained size does — default to 0, or
be an error at first use as the interpreter does, with the six library
declarations that carry dead sizes as the test case
(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c; `array-design-review.md` finding 7); whether
arithmetic inside white brackets is refused as ill-formed, which three library
storing objects would then fail (`array-design-review.md` finding 5); and
whether the checker rung is scheduled before or after a shadow session has
shown where the crash actually lives (`array-design-review.md` §1b).

## 9. Glossary

**AST** — abstract syntax tree; here, the classes under `nodes/`, generated
from `astgen/Fortress.ast`, and the only intermediate representation in either
path (`modules-and-phases.md` B.1).

**api / component** — the two kinds of compilation unit: an api is an interface
(`.fsi`), a component an implementation (`.fss`). Their analysed forms are
cached as `.tfi` and `.tfs` (`repository/ProjectProperties.java:319, 323`).

**bidirectional checking** — checking an expression with an expected type
pushed down into it, rather than only reading a type out; the second argument
of `checkExpr` (`typechecker/STypeChecker.scala:405-419`).

**bytecode cache** — `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache`, one jar per
compiled component, and the first entry on the run class path
(`NamingCzar.java:132`, `bin/run_classpath:26`).

**candidate set** — the list of functions a name could refer to, attached to a
reference by the disambiguator; there are two, and the paths read different
ones (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`).

**desugaring** — a tree-to-tree rewrite that replaces a surface construct with
a simpler one; three phases of it here, gated by switches on `Shell`
(section 4).

**gate** — the check a change must pass: `ant testFast` (about 1,377 tests) and
`ant testSystem` (382), zero failures, on a clean build
(`protocol.md` §6).

**IntArg / IntExpr / IntRef / IntBase** — the AST nodes a size travels in: an
`IntArg` holds an `IntExpr`, which is a literal (`IntBase`), a symbol
(`IntRef`) or an arithmetic node (`Fortress.ast:1275-1348`).

**`nat` parameter** — a static parameter whose argument is a number rather than
a type; a size in a type (section 8).

**phase** — one named step in the list built from `PhaseOrder`; the two paths
are two arrays in one file (`phases/PhaseOrder.java:125-147`).

**prelude** — the library a world links without an import: `FortressLibrary` +
`FortressBuiltin` + `AnyType` for the interpreter, `CompilerLibrary` +
`CompilerBuiltin` + `AnyType` for the compiler
(`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:113-137`).

**sayWhat** — the code generator's refusal: `Can't compile <node>`, thrown from
`defaultCase` for any node with no visitor (`CodeGen.java:1551-1553`,
`:1668-1670`).

**shadow** — a way to prototype an edit to the sealed tree without changing it:
compile edited copies of the files and put the class files first on the class
path (`map/README.md` §0; FACTS, the template-checking fix).

**static parameter / static argument** — what stands between white brackets in
a declaration (`[\T, nat s0\]`) and in a use (`[\RR64, 16\]`). Five kinds
exist; the checker implements two (`STypesUtil.scala:546-559`).

**stamping** — producing a class for one instantiation of a generic by
rewriting a template's bytes at class-load time; it renames and does not change
representation (`Instantiater.java:47-58`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.11).

**template (two senses)** — in syntax abstraction, the body of a grammar rule
with holes in it (section 2); in code generation, the single class emitted for
a generic declaration and stamped at load time (sections 5 and 6). They are
unrelated.

**world** — which prelude a run links against; set per subcommand by
`useCompilerLibraries` / `useInterpreterLibraries`
(`Shell.java:371-386`).

## 1. What an array is in the interpreter today

An array is a trait, not a primitive. `Array[\E,I\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1322`) is generic in the element type `E` and the index type `I` (`ZZ32` for rank 1, `(ZZ32,ZZ32)` for rank 2) and carries no size in its type. Its protocol is `get(i)` and `put(i, v)`; subscripting is sugar for them (`opr[i:I]:=(v:E) = put(offset(i),v)`, `FortressLibrary.fss:1886-1889`). `ReadableArray` (`.fsi:1247`) is the read half; `Indexed` (`.fsi:1111`) makes every array a generator, so `for x <- a` and `BIG +` work over it.

Sizes enter one layer up. `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]` (`.fsi:1435`), `Array2` (`.fss:2289`) and `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, nat b1, nat s1, nat b2, nat s2\]` (`.fsi:1652`) put the lower bound and size of each dimension into the type. `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` (`.fsi:1460`) is an `Array1` that is also an additive group (`+`, `-`, unary `-`, `zero`, plus `scale`, `pmul`, `dot`); `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` (`.fsi:1578`) is an `Array2` with `mul[\nat s2\]`, `rmul`, `lmul`, `t()`. Both exclude the multiplicative ring because juxtaposition is the inner product (FACTS, the library's arrays and algebra).

Storage is one object per rank-1 array, holding boxed values. `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]` (`LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:15-27`) binds `get`, `put` and `init0` to Java glue; the glue allocates an `AtomicArray` of the evaluator's boxed `FValue`s (`interpreter/glue/prim/PrimitiveArray.java:35, 44-56`; `evaluator/transactions/AtomicArray.java:23`). A rank-2 array is a rank-1 array with the index folded as `i s1 + j`, row by row (`__DefaultArray2`, `FortressLibrary.fss:2415-2421`); rank 3 the same. So the interpreter's arrays are already flat, row-major storage under a trait; what they are not is unboxed. One exception exists and nothing uses it: `PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\]` over a Java `double[]` (`NativeArray.fss:41-51`; `glue/prim/PrimImmutableRR64Array.java:40`), referenced by no library file.

The everyday operations are Fortress loops over `get`/`put`. `fill(f)` is `for i <- zeroIndices() do init0(i, f(toIndex(i))) end` (`.fss:1974-1976`); `map(f)` and `ivmap(f)` (map with the index) make a `replica` of the same shape and `fill` it (`.fss:2135-2138`); `t()` returns a transposed view, not a copy (`.fss:2395` for `Array2`, `:2559` for `Matrix`). The whole protocol runs from `trait Indexed` at `.fss:1636` to the end of `SubArray3` at `:2808`, about 1,170 lines, plus the 54 lines of `NativeArray.fss` and the integer-only scalar extension at `.fss:4477-4517`.

A run-time size becomes a type by reflection. `array[\E\](x: ZZ32)` (`.fss:1922`) calls `reflect(x)`, which returns a value of type `N[\n\]` with the number baked into the nat (`LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`), and `__arr1[\E, nat n\](…, x: N[\n\])` (`.fss:1930`) then builds an `Array1[\E,0,n\]`. The interpreter can do this because a nat is a type in its own lattice, made at run time (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java`).

A nat is checked at run time, at dispatch, and only then. When a call meets a nat parameter, a literal must be equal and a symbol is bound (`IntNat.unifyStaticArg`, `IntNat.java:127-147`); a mismatch is "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (FACTS, execution model, last bullet). Nothing is optimised on a nat anywhere.

## 2. What the compiled world has

The compiler's own library is small: `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` 778 lines with a 1,627-line body, `CompilerLibrary.fsi` 356 with 718. It has no `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` or `Matrix` with a body. The one `nat` declaration in it is `trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\] extends Object end` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:279`), empty.

It has exactly one numeric array, and it is the shape the 2012 team chose for this world. `trait ZZ32Vector` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:555-572`) has no static parameters at all: `shape`, `nrows`, `ncols`, `copy`, `opr[i]`, `opr[i,j]`, their `:=` forms, `|self|`, `fill`, `fill2`. Its body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1101-1136`) forwards every member to Java helpers imported at `.fss:299-305`. The Java class `FZZ32Vector` holds an unboxed `int[]` and four shape integers (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java:18-19`); a 2-D index is folded to `(i-lower_x)*dim_y + (j-lower_y)` (`:65`); the whole class is 83 lines and its helper `nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java` 40. `NamingCzar` lists it as a special type whose implementation class is hand-written (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:553`, in the table declared at `:508-514`; also `:337-338` and `:461`). Above it, `CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535` declares `PREFIX_SUM`, `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX` with a scalar, each a Fortress `for` loop over subscripts, and factories at `:587-593`. `StringVector` is the same design over `String[]` (`FStringVector.java:16`). Three live tests: `other_compiler_tests/VectorTest.fss`, `VectorTest2.fss`, `VectorTest3.fss`.

An element read on that unboxed vector still boxes. Verified in bytecode (§9, probe 2): `v[0]` compiles to a virtual call `FZZ32Vector."[]"(FZZ32) → FZZ32`, which calls `getValue`, which calls the generated native wrapper, which unwraps the index with `FZZ32.getValue()`, calls `simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, int) → int`, and re-wraps the result with `FZZ32.make(int)`; the caller then `checkcast`s. Four calls and one allocation per element. The storage is unboxed; the traffic is not.

The code generator lowers every type to a reference. `RR64` is `FRR64` (`NamingCzar.java:441-446` maps the bare JVM `double` to `RR64` only at the foreign-Java boundary); `x y` on two `RR64` is an interface call on `FRR64`, no `dmul` (`perf-probes/boxing/javap/CompilerBuiltin.juxtaposition_RR64.javap.txt:3559-3565`). The subscript node has no code-generation case of its own: `CodeGen.forSubscriptExpr` throws if reached (`codegen/CodeGen.java:4931`), so every `a[i]` is desugared into a method call on the array's trait before code generation.

Stamping renames; it cannot change a representation. Verified (§9, probe 1): the template for `object Box[\T\](x: T)` has the field `x` with descriptor `LT;`; the stamped `Box⟦FRR64⟧` has `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64;`. The substitution replaces one class name with another inside a reference descriptor. `[D` is not a class name, so no instantiation of a generic template can produce a `double[]` field, and the stamped interface's `get` returns the boxed class. The place the team left for anything cleverer is `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }` at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`.

The checker does not implement `nat` parameters, and the code generator carries them in names only; §6 has the full account. In one line each, verified (§9, probes 3-6): a nat passed explicitly to a function that uses it in no type compiles and runs; a nat that must be inferred from an argument is `Not yet implemented`; a nat-parameterised object instantiated with a literal crashes the checker with `ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr`; a nat used as a value inside a function compiles to a reference to a class that does not exist and dies at run time. So sized array types cannot be declared on this path until the second fork lands, and unsized ones can be declared today.

The generic generator protocol exists here: `Generator[\E1\]` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:614`) and `Reduction[\R\]` (`:638`). What is missing for arrays is `Indexed` and everything below it.

## 3. What microGPT needs from arrays

The vocabulary is `explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi`, inventoried in `reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §1 at the committed version `a92569f83`: 38 declarations, of which 5 are aliases of library calls, 26 are new operations over the library's own array types, and 9 are new structures. (The working copy is under uncommitted repair after that review; Pavol's position of 2026-09-19 is that the model's operators stay operators and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, `POSITIONS.md:38`, so the 26 stay operators and the compile path's overloading check must let them stand beside the prelude's `+`, `MAX` and juxtaposition, which is unmeasured.)

The 26 operations, by what they do to the data. Elementwise maps, 14: `+` and `-` with a scalar in both orders (4), the elementwise product `×`, `/` array by array and array by scalar (2), `MAX` with a scalar (2), `>` giving 0/1, `SQRT`, `exp`, `log`, and the broadcast add of a matrix to every plane of a rank-3 array (review rows 5-17 and 30). Contractions, meaning sums of products such as a matrix product, 2: the row scaling `diag(v) m` (row 20) and the plane-wise batched product of two rank-3 arrays (row 29); the 16×16 matrix product itself and `DOT` are the shipped library's own (`FortressLibrary.fss:2621-2629`) and are what the kernels time. Structural, 10: the row lift `rows(f, m)` in four shapes (31-34), `gather`, `onehot`, `pick`, `flat` (35-38) and the two transposes `^T` (39-40). The 9 structures are views: `Diag`, the transposed rank-3 array, the matrix over a slice of the flat parameter vector (`PView`), the row and plane-row views, and `heads`/`unheads`/`plane`, each a six-line object whose `get`/`put` index another array (review §1, last paragraph).

Element types needed: `RR64` for every weight and activation, `ZZ32` for keys and the integer corpus, `Char`/`String` for the corpus text in `FlatData`. Sizes: the hyperparameters are literals bound to names (`MicroGptFlat.fss:17`: 16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26); the flat parameter vector's 4192 is computed; every constructor takes a run-time size and returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` or `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]` (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17` at `a92569f83`); nat-typed values enter through views built with `reflect` (`PView[\nat s, nat r, nat c\]`, `viewN(…, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))`, `:54-62`) and through the model's `Matrix`/`Array3` declarations: 20 of the api's declarations carry a nat, 25 in the focused base's `FlatArrays2.fsi`.

The measured cost of boxing on these shapes (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` §2; Java models of the runtime's own box, `Box[]` storage, against `double[]`): the 4192-element dot product 6.26× slower boxed, the 16×16 matrix product 6.53×, the row lift with `rmsn` 2.59×. The generic array object on top (an `Object[]` behind an interface with a `checkcast` per read) adds 9 %, 1.6 % and 4.8 %. The cost is the element boxes, not the container's genericity. None of the three kernels compiles today: 77 errors, `Array`, `Vector`, `Array3` undefined, all raised inside `FlatArrays.fsi`. All eighteen components of the two microGPT programs stop at disambiguation on `Array` (8), `Char` (5), `ImmutableArray` (3), `Vector` (2) (`compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.md`); on the ladder, 42 files stop first on an array name (`ImmutableArray` 26, `Array1` 6, `Array` 6, `Array2` 2, the factory `array` 2; counted from `baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv`).

## 4. The options as they stood before the rulings

Option (a), the interpreter's protocol ported boxed, is closed by Pavol's first ruling (§6) and is kept here only so the record shows what was rejected: about 1,200 lines of trait layer moved into `CompilerLibrary` over an `Object[]` native class; the fastest route to "the kernels compile"; the 6.3-6.5× kept; unboxing afterwards a second storage class under the same traits, "the same library written twice" (`map/README.md:127`).

### (b) `double[]`-backed arrays with unboxed elements designed in

What is built: `FRR64Vector.java` beside `FZZ32Vector.java`, the same 83 lines with `double[] val` and the four shape integers; `simpleDoubleVector.java` beside `simpleIntVector.java`; a trait in `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` with the nine members of `ZZ32Vector`; one line in `NamingCzar`'s special table and one in its foreign-route chain; a factory. That is the team's own five wiring sites. `ZZ32Vector` already covers the integer keys; `StringVector` the corpus.

Its own class, not a stamped instance: §2 verified that stamping substitutes class names into reference descriptors, so no instantiation of a generic template can hold a `double[]`; the `RR64` store is a hand-written class, as `FZZ32Vector` is, and anything reached through a generic trait's `get` is boxed at that boundary.

What the code generator must learn, if the loops are to run unboxed in generated code: an element read must become `getfield val:[D`, `iload i`, `daload` instead of the four-call chain of §2, and a bare `double` must have somewhere to go, which means a local variable slot of descriptor `D` and `dadd`/`dmul` for `RR64` arithmetic whenever the checker's static type is `RR64`, boxing only where a value meets a `T` or an `Any`. That is unboxing by static type (`performance-roadmap.md` A1) in `CodeGen.java` (6,750 lines) and `VarCodeGen`; every rung of it is a `.java` rung under the full gate with the 85 files as the net. Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured, and the Java model that would answer it is one more class in `perf-probes/kernels/java/`.

A second route to unboxed loops needs no code-generator change: write the loops of the vocabulary's operations as Java natives over `double[]` (the dot product, the matrix product, the elementwise maps, `SQRT`/`exp`/`log` over an array), so a box is paid once per whole-array operation instead of once per element. This is the shape of an APL implementation, each primitive a native loop, and microGPT in the C4 form is whole-array vocabulary; the residue is the user lambdas passed to `fill`, `map` and `rows`, which box per element. Not the team's precedent: their `ZZ32Vector` operators are Fortress loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`).

As first written, (b) carried sizes as run-time fields only and no nat in the type; Pavol's second ruling (§6) removes that half, so what survives of (b) is the store class and the two routes to unboxed loops, under the library's sized traits of §6.

### (c) The library's generic traits over per-element-type native stores

What is built: the interpreter's trait layer, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array[\E,I\]`, `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, `Array3`, with `fill`, `map`, `ivmap`, `t()` and the views written in Fortress as they are in `FortressLibrary.fss`; beneath them, in the place of `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]` (`__DefaultVector`'s `mem` field, `.fss:2204-2205`), one hand-written native store per element type: the `double[]` class of (b) for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, a boxed `Object[]` store for every other `T`. The checker sees the library's own types; the model's `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, `Vector[\RR64,s\]`, `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` resolve as written.

What selects the store. Not the checker: it has no notion of representation. The factory does, from the run-time type tag: a generic instantiation carries its arguments as run-time type descriptors (probe 1's `Box$RTTIc` holds a field `T` of type `RTTI`), so a native helper behind `array1[\T, nat s0\]()` can return the `double[]` store when `T`'s tag is `FRR64` and the boxed store otherwise, which is `performance-roadmap.md` A2's "class tag". Alternatively the vocabulary's `vec`/`mat` make the `RR64` store directly, which is what `FlatArrays.fss:14-17` already does through `array[\RR64\](n)`.

How a hand-written class sits under a stamped generic trait: `FZZ32Vector extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32Vector.DefaultTraitMethods implements ZZ32Vector` (`FZZ32Vector.java:16-17`), a non-generic Fortress trait whose generated abstract class the Java extends. So the store's trait must be non-generic (`RR64Store`), declared in Fortress as extending the generic `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, and the generated abstract class then carries the stamped supertype. Unprobed: that a non-generic trait extending an instantiated generic supertype with a hand-written implementation class compiles and links; it is the first thing the array rung of §8 finds out.

Can Fortress's overloading express the specialisation? Not as two top-level declarations of one operator: `opr +[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64)` beside `opr +(a: RR64Store, s: RR64)` is one declaration with a static parameter and one without, forbidden by `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105` and refused by the interpreter's check (the review's probe A). It is expressible as one declaration over the trait whose work is done by the object's own methods (`get`, `put`, `dot`, the product), which is the interpreter's own idiom for views (`TransposedMatrix`, `FortressLibrary.fss:2571-2588`) and ordinary virtual dispatch. Through the trait every `get` still boxes at the boundary; unboxed loops exist only inside the store's native methods (the second route of (b)) or after the code generator learns to unbox (the first route of (b)).

Cost: one `.java` rung (store class, factory helper, the non-generic store trait, full gate), one library rung (the trait layer in Fortress, `testFast` alone), then the native operations as in (b); all of it after or beside the nat rung of §6, because `Array1` and `Vector` cannot be declared before it. What it forecloses: nothing named; `ImmutableArray` (26 ladder files, through `List.fsi`) needs the immutable variant in every option.

## 5. What the specification and the team's own drafts say

The specification's array is a family of sized types over a generic one, and it keeps both factories. The type of a k-dimensional array expression is `Array k[T, 0, n0, …, 0, n_{k-1}]`, abbreviated `T[n0, …]`, with a footnote that "As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides Array k types for 1 ≤ k ≤ 3" (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:130-136`); a two-dimensional array of numbers "is a matrix", a one-dimensional one "is a vector", with the editors' margin notes reading "can be coerced to a matrix" (`:152-170`). The factory table gives `array[E](size)` for "the specified runtime-determined size" and `array1[E,n]()` for "statically determined size n" side by side (`advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`).

On storage: "As in Fortran, Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), with the note that distributions and `HeapSequence` "are not yet supported" (`:15-16`). Nothing in the prose says boxed or unboxed; the intent is an array as a structure over a linear store, which (c) is.

On sizes in types: "types can be parametric with respect to other types and values (most notably natural numbers)" (`preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:85-86`); the nat chapter is quoted in §6.

On the intended aggregate: "Guy's proposal for making tensors the principal user-level indexed aggregate type in Fortress (06/27/07)" and his email "Arrays, matrices, and tensors (short)" of 12/15/06 (`appendices/future.tex:63-65`); the FAQ's answer to variable-sized arrays with static bounds checking is a link to a wiki page that no longer exists (`appendices/FAQ.tex:55-57`); the emails themselves are not in the repository (`map/design-intent-sources.md:111, 128`).

On the compiled encoding: the JVM paper says "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds in domain and range" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping is a renaming, and that the template's side file "contains info about the static parameters, including their names, whether they are types, oprs, or nats" (`:142`), which the tree does (§6). The team's own unboxing note is `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:18-30`: four cases, "primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean", singleton objects, unboxed fields, "comprises unboxed"; a taxonomy referenced by nothing.

The drafts say nothing about arrays. `Library/incomplete/` (24 files) contains no mention of an array. `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (783 lines, imported by nothing) are the generator and reduction protocol, `Container`, `DefaultGeneratorImplementation`, without `Indexed` or any array. `Fortress.Operators.fsi.INCOMPLETE` is the algebra above `Number` and names no aggregate. What the team shipped in this world is `ZZ32Vector`, and it is the only precedent with code behind it.

## 6. The nat plan: what the second fork must deliver for the first

Pavol's rulings of 2026-09-19, in his words. On boxing: "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." On sizes: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." So the sized types are built as the team designed them, `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]`, the checker is taught nat parameters, and the two forks are taken together. On method: "study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way"; microGPT's operations go into the standard library in its spirit, not into a user file.

### 6a. What the checker and the code generator lack today

Inference. `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` answers `NI.nyi()` for `KindInt`, `KindBool`, `KindDim`, `KindUnit` and `KindNat` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:546-559`), so any call whose nat must be worked out from an argument, `same(x, y)` with `same[\nat n\](a: Vec[\n\], b: Vec[\n\])`, dies with `Not yet implemented` (probe 5). Every product in the library is such a call (`opr DOT[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\]`).

Equality. `pEqv(IntArg, IntArg)` is `pTrue()` under the team's comment "Not handling all static args properly yet" (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:327-337`): today any two nat arguments are equal, `Vector[\T,3\]` is `Vector[\T,4\]`. Exclusion has the matching hole, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args" (`:447-451`). Export checking compares an api's and a component's declarations with `equalIntExprs`, which is `= false` with the comment "Not implemented!" (`scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:640-648`), so every exported signature mentioning `Vector[\T,n\]` fails the export check once the crashes are gone.

Objects. `object Vec[\nat n\](v: ZZ32Vector)` instantiated as `Vec[\4\](…)`, with no `extends` and no use of `n`, crashes with `ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr` (probe 4), in the method gathering that composes one static-argument replacer with another (`STypesUtil.scala:1536-1548`, `compiler/typechecker/StaticTypeReplacer.java:95-99, 102, 121-128, 221-223`): somewhere the nat `n` is held as a type argument `TypeArg(VarType n)` and a later `IntArg(IntRef n)` receives a `VarType` where an integer expression is required. The disambiguator does rewrite a known nat's argument from `TypeArg` to `IntArg` (`compiler/disambiguator/TypeDisambiguator.java:402-433`, with its comment "TODO: shouldn't there be a NatArg class?"; `:663-697`, "All Args are parsed as TypeArgs"); which path escapes it was not found by reading, here or in `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §c.

Code generation. A nat in value position, `foo[\nat n\](): ZZ32 = n.asZZ32 + 1`, compiles, and the call sites are stamped as `foo⟦5⟧` and `foo⟦4192⟧` (probe 6), because the name mangler carries a nat literal or symbol into the instantiation name (`NamingCzar.java:1891-1911`, the kind tag `intnat`, `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:213`) and the template's side file records the kind (`function 1 6 intnat 1 n`). But the template body reads `n` as `getstatic NatVal$n.ONLY`, a top-level variable class that does not exist, and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: NatVal$n`. The loader treats only the operator kind specially (`Naming.java:98`) and substitutes names; nothing turns a nat in a name back into a value. An `IntArg` in an `extends` clause throws `CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")` (`codegen/CodeGen.java:5783-5792`), which every `object … extends Vector[\RR64,s\]` will hit. `compiler_tests/Compiled1.av.fss` declares the value use and never calls it, which is why the gate is green over it.

What already works: an explicit nat argument to a function that uses it in no type (probe 3; `compiler_tests/Compiled1.p.fss`, `Compiled6.af.fss`); a nat in value position types as an integer literal (`typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:64-70`, the spec's "any context a variable of type N32 can appear"); the instantiation walker already substitutes `IntRef` (`STypesUtil.scala:627-679`, per the plan).

### 6b. What the team wrote, and what the interpreter does

The chapter opens "Non-type static parameters and static expressions are not yet supported. The examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter." (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:15-17`). The semantics: "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values. A nat parameter may be used to instantiate other nat parameters, or to appear in any context that a variable of type N32 can appear, except that it cannot be assigned to." (`:82-86`). The one example is `makeVector`, "a nat parameter s0, which appears in both the parameter type and return type" (`:94-97`). Static expressions in types (`n+1`) are "not yet supported" (`basic/expressions/constant.tex:15`) and only "a restricted subset of operations" may occur as static arguments (`:17-25`), never listed.

The internal meeting record (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex:160-217`) decided: overloading `T[\n+1\]` against `T[\0\]` is "Not allowed" (`:167-182`); `T[\1\]` against `T[\0\]` is "Allowed" because "nat parameters are all instantiated" (`:183-198`); `ZZ32` against `T[\0\]` is "Allowed" "if our implementation strategy for nat parameters is 'don't instantiate'" (`:199-208`), the one recorded implementation stance; mutually recursive nat-arithmetic extends clauses are out by acyclicity (`:210-217`). The JVM paper planned to carry nats through templates by name (`MethodMapping.tex:142`), which is what the mangler and the side file do.

The interpreter has the whole run-time half. A nat is a type interned per value (`IntNat.java`); a static argument is evaluated, `+`, `-` and juxtaposition included (`interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:431-464`); at a call, `unifyStaticArg` requires a literal to be equal, binds a symbol, and errors on anything else (`IntNat.java:127-147`); an unbound parameter becomes `BottomType` (`EvaluatorBase.java:238-240`); the unification runs at every call (`EvaluatorBase.java:88-176`). So the checker's job is the interpreter's `unifyStaticArg` moved to compile time: symbols and literals, equality, no arithmetic, which is also the letter of the meeting record.

### 6c. How the library's own nat declarations use them (92 lines in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 81 declarations; `NativeArray.fss` 3; `NatReflect.fss` 2)

Rank tags: `Rank[\nat n\]`, `Indexed1/2/3[\nat n\]` (`.fss:1592, 1612-1616`); the nat is a marker in the type and never a value.

Every one of these is a symbol or a literal; no arithmetic occurs inside white brackets anywhere in the library or in the two microGPT programs (`nat-checking-plan.md` §d census). So the minimal checker, symbols and literals unified by equality, covers all 81 and all of microGPT's, with the reflection group needing one more thing (§6d).

### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array

Where the nat lives, two places, both needed: in the stamped class's name, `Vector⟦FRR64,16⟧` and `Vector⟦FRR64,4192⟧` being different classes, which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6) and which is what makes the nat a fact for the checker and for dispatch; and as a run-time field of the native store (`dim_x` in the `FZZ32Vector` shape), because nothing today turns the name back into a value, the store's `get`, `put` and `|self|` need the number, and the `double[]` carries its own length. One class per distinct size is the price; microGPT's sizes are six literals and a computed 4192.

What the loader must do with a nat argument beyond what it does: supply a value for a nat in value position inside a template. Either the instantiater rewrites the `getstatic <Component>$n.ONLY` reference into a constant when it stamps `⟦…,5,…⟧` (an instruction-level substitution in `Instantiater`, the job the expando stub at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172` was left for), or the code generator emits a read from the run-time type descriptor, which today refuses `IntArg` (`CodeGen.java:5783`). Under the two-place representation the library's value uses of a nat are few (`i s1 + j` in `__DefaultArray2`, the `N[\s0\]` witness in `subarray`) and the store's field can serve the first; the second is explicit-only. So the value mechanism is a `.java` rung of its own, needed for the full port and not for the first kernels. Default: the field first, the name-to-constant substitution when the port reaches `subarray`.

Run-time sizes: `array[\RR64\](n)` with `n` computed cannot name its class at compile time. Either a native helper builds the stamped name from the integer and asks the loader for `Array1⟦FRR64,0,4192⟧` by that string, which is a string from a number and unprobed, or the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17`) and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes. Default: the second; it is what the model writes today, and the `reflect` group of §6c is then the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce until the first is probed.

## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed

Question 1, boxed or `double[]`: closed by Pavol, `double[]`. Consequence: the `RR64` store is a hand-written class on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic (§2), and the boxed `Object[]` store exists only for element types that have no native store.

Question 4, where sizes live: closed by Pavol, in the type as the team designed. Consequences: the checker rung of §6e precedes the first sized declaration; the export checker and the object crash are on the path, not optional; every distinct size is a stamped class; the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array` until the string-from-number route is probed (§6d, default).

Question 2, open: what implements the library's sized traits under `double[]`?
Branch "native stores per element type under the library's generic objects": `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag; the interpreter's own layering with `PrimitiveArray` replaced; one unprobed link, the non-generic store trait under the generic `Array` (§4c).
Branch "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation": the expando route; `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,4192⟧` would load a different class than `PrimitiveArray⟦FZZ32,4192⟧`; nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution.
Default: the first; it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure.

Question 3, open: where do the loops run unboxed?
Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; the user lambdas of `fill`, `map`, `rows` still box per element.
Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.

Question 5, open, from the third ruling: the library's unused nats (`.fsi:1496-1523`). Branch "default an unconstrained nat to `0`" keeps the library's text; branch "refuse and delete the dead parameters" edits six library declarations. Default: the first, the plan's own recommendation, and the only reason the checker rung would otherwise touch `Library/`.

Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.

# Review of the array design for the compiled world

## 0. What was checked and how

The design's own citations were opened: every line number in §1, §2, §4c, §5, §6a-§6e and §8 was read in the tree, and the two rulings were read in `POSITIONS.md:40`. Where the design says "unprobed" or "not measured", or where a claim depends on what the checker does rather than on what the interpreter does, a probe was run: five Fortress programs through `fortress compile` under a private cache (one also through the interpreter), and two Java models beside the kernel models of `perf-probes/kernels/java`. Nothing under `default_repository/`, `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/` was touched.

The standard applied is the one in the brief: finish what the designers intended, judged by the July 2012 draft and the breadcrumbs in all three sources of truth (specification, interpreter and its library, compiler and its prelude); storage is `double[]`, unboxed; sizes are `nat` parameters and the two forks are taken together; extensions go into the standard library in the library's own patterns; and the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled and running fast.

## 1. Findings

### Decisive 1. The design keeps the model's unsized static types and never checks the model's applications against a static checker; as written, nothing in microGPT and none of the three kernels passes the type checker, whatever the storage is

What the design says. §3: "every constructor takes a run-time size and returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` or `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]`"; §6d, default: "the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model … and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes"; §6c: the minimal checker "covers all 81 and all of microGPT's" declarations; §8: the second rung times "`kdot` compiled over a native `dot`".

What the model is. `rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\])` computes `x DOT x` (`run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:27`); `DOT` exists only on `Vector[\T,n\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2264-2265`, and the api `.fsi:1508`); `FlatArrays` declares no `DOT`. `view(p, i)` returns `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]` (`:45`), `wq^T` needs `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` (`:23`), and `x1 wq^T` (`:58`) is the library's juxtaposition on two `Matrix` (`.fss:2625-2627`); `x1` comes from `rows`, which returns `Array` (`FlatArrays.fss:139`). `diag(vm / nv)` (`:63`) passes an `Array` where `diag` takes `Vector[\RR64,s\]` (`FlatArrays.fss:41`); `gather(wte, ids)` (`:57`) passes the `Array` from `view` where `gather` takes `Matrix`; `rows(rmsn, x)` (`:57`) passes the `Array` from `gather + gather` where `rows` takes `Matrix`. The kernels are the same: `kdot.fss` writes `x DOT y` on two `vec(…)` results typed `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` (`FlatArrays.fss:14`); `kmat.fss` writes `a b` on two `mat(…)` results; `krows.fss` writes `rows(rmsn, m)` on a `mat(…)` result.

Why it runs on the interpreter. `array[\E\](n)` reflects `n` into a nat and calls `array1[\E,n\]()` (`.fss:1927-1934`), which selects `vector[\T,s0\]()` for any `Number` by `typecase` (`:2240-2244`), so the run-time object behind every `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` in the model is a `__DefaultVector[\RR64,n\]`, a `Vector`, and the interpreter dispatches on the run-time object; the static type is never consulted (FACTS, execution model: the checker "runs only on the compile path"). The same holds for the views: `view` calls `viewN(p, off, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))` (`FlatArrays.fss:60-62`), where `reflect` returns `NatParam` (`LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`) and `viewN` takes `N[\r\]`; only the run-time object is an `N[\16\]`.

What the checker does with it. Probe `p3_static_dispatch.fss`, no `nat` in it so nothing else can be what fails: a trait `Vec[\T\] extends Arr[\T\]`, an object under `Vec[\RR64\]`, a function on two `Vec[\RR64\]`, and a call on a value whose static type is `Arr[\RR64\]`. Compile path: `(Vec[\RR64\], Vec[\RR64\])->RR64 is not applicable to an argument of type (Arr[\RR64\], Arr[\RR64\])`, exit 255 (`p3_static_dispatch.compile.out`); interpreter, same file: `p3 9.0` (`p3_static_dispatch.interp.out`). As an operator the refusal is identical and lists the prelude's scalar `DOT` overloads beside the user's (`p3b_static_dispatch_opr.compile.out`).

Where the first compiled microGPT fails, then. Before the model: `FlatArrays.fss:62`, `viewN(p, off, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))`, because `NatParam` is not `N[\r\]` statically and the checker cannot infer `r` from a run-time object. Then `MicroGptFlat.fss:27` on `x DOT x`, and after that nearly every line of `step` (`:57-70`). The design's own second-rung measurement, `kdot` through a native `dot`, cannot happen as written: `kdot.fss:15` is `x DOT y` on two unsized `Array`s.

Why this is decisive. The two rulings of 2026-09-19 (`POSITIONS.md:38, 40`) are "the model's text is the notation" and "nat sizes are central, not sidestepped"; on the compile path these two collide on every operator application in the model, because the model's text carries sizes only in its run-time objects. The design says "the checker sees the library's own types; the model's `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, `Vector[\RR64,s\]`, `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` resolve as written" (§4c); the types resolve, the applications do not. That collision is not named anywhere in the 203 lines, and it is the first decision Pavol has to take (§2, decision D), not a repair a rung can make.

### Decisive 2. The default for "what implements the sized traits over the store" has no checked mechanism on this path; the checker refuses it, including through the library's own selection idiom

What the design says. §4c and §7 question 2, default: `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` "keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag … it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure"; "a native helper behind `array1[\T, nat s0\]()` can return the `double[]` store when `T`'s tag is `FRR64` and the boxed store otherwise".

What the probes say. `p1_monostore.fss`: a generic `Arr[\T\]`, a monomorphic `DStore extends Arr[\RR64\]`, and `mk[\T\](x: T): Arr[\T\] = DStore()`. Refused: `Function body has type DStore, but declared return type is Arr[\T\]` (`p1_monostore.compile.out`). `p1b_typecase.fss`, the library's own idiom from `array1` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2240-2244`), `typecase w of () -> RR64 => DStore() else => BStore[\T\](x) end`: refused, `Function body has type OR(DStore,BStore[\T\]), but declared return type is Arr[\T\]` (`p1b_typecase.compile.out`). The library's `array1` passes the interpreter because nothing checks it, and would pass the checker only because both of its arms (`vector[\T,s0\]()`, `PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]()`) stay generic in `T`; a `double[]` store is not generic in `T`, which is the whole point of it.

What "the library's own structure" would have to become. A generic object cannot have a field whose type changes with `T`; `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]` is one type. So the shape is one monomorphic storing object per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]() extends Vector[\RR64,s0\]` with `mem: RR64Store`) beside the generic boxed one, and the problem moves to the factory `vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]()`, which must return the monomorphic object for `T = RR64` inside a body the checker types with `T` abstract; the probes show it cannot. A foreign helper cannot be generic (`import java` binds static methods with fixed types, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:300-306`); a second factory name per element type is the library's pattern for `array1`/`vector` (`.fss:2251`) but does not make `vector[\RR64,16\]()` produce the store; a code-generator special case in the manner of `NamingCzar`'s hand-implemented types (`NamingCzar.java:538-553`) is a `.java` change. Every route is a `.java` rung; "no loader change" is not one of them.

The branch the design dismissed is the team's. §7's second branch, "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation", is set aside as "nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution". The team's breadcrumbs point there: `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` lists as case 1 "primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean" and as case 3 "unboxed fields"; the expando stub `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }` is in the loader (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`); the JVM paper's stamping by upper bound (`MethodMapping.tex:134`) is the mechanism that would be specialised. `PLAN.md` step 5 says of this exact item "the probe on generic instantiation in the class loader comes first"; the design's probe 1 shows what the loader does today, not whether it can select, and the plan's probe was not run. Our own roadmap's A2 ("selected from the element type carried at run time. Scala's `Array[Double]` via class tags", `performance-roadmap.md:40`) is the design's default; the team's direction is the other branch. Which precedent wins is Pavol's (§2, decision A).

### Decisive 3. The second reserved fork, the library route, is closed by default in §7, against the ruling as it was applied the same evening

What the design says. §7, last paragraph: "Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style"; §4c and §8: the interpreter's trait layer "written in Fortress as they are in `FortressLibrary.fss`" into the compiler world.

What the ruling said and did. `POSITIONS.md:39`: "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." The commit that applied it, `02d09a39f` (`postmortem-2026-09-19/array-work-brief.md` §1), edited `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, the interpreter's library. `PLAN.md`, stop conditions: what stops the climb includes "the library route, the interpreter's library as prelude against growing the compiler library beyond what one rung needs". `next-climb.md` §3a: "the second reserved fork — the library route … is entangled with it".

What building in the compiler world means, which the design does not say. ### Serious 4. "Natives first" contradicts the ruling's letter, has no team precedent, and is measured to deliver nothing on the shapes the model is made of

What the design says. §7 question 3, default: "natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4"; §4b admits "Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured".

Measured now (`compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`, the kernels' harness, medians of 3). Unboxed `double[]` storage read and written through a boxing accessor, arithmetic boxed as the runtime boxes it: `kdot` 0.007559 s, 8.9× primitive, against boxed storage 0.005495 s (6.4×) and primitive 0.000852 s; `kmat` 0.005552 s, 6.6×, against boxed 0.005255 s (6.2×) and primitive 0.000844 s. The store buys nothing until the traffic is unboxed; the design's §2 already showed the traffic on `ZZ32Vector` is four calls and an allocation per element (probe 2).

Where the model's traffic is. The model's data design is views: nine `PView`s over the flat vector, `RowView`, `Row3View`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane`, `Diag`, `Transposed3` (`FlatArrays.fss:40-120`), each a `get` that indexes another array. A native product over a view reads its operand through `get`, boxed; a native `dot` over the store helps `p DOT p` and Adam's three lines (`MicroGptFlat.fss:76-79`) and nothing in `step`. So the first rung's number (`kdot` over a store) would not transfer to the program the number is for.

Precedent. The team's compiler-world operators over `ZZ32Vector` are Fortress `for` loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`), and the team's unboxing note is a code-generator taxonomy (`Unbox.java`); the design says of natives "Not the team's precedent" (§4b) and defaults to them anyway. The route with the precedent, and the only one under which "it cannot be boxed" is true of the model, is unboxing by static type in generated code (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1), which is the largest code-generator work in the plan. Decision B.

### Serious 7. The unconstrained-nat default is unsafe and does not address what the export checker will actually meet

The design (§7 question 5, default): "default an unconstrained nat to `0`", keeping the library's text at `.fsi:1496-1523`.

What those six declarations are. The api declares `opr +[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m\](me: Vector[\T,n\], other: Vector[\T,n\])` and `-` with a dead `m` (`.fsi:1496-1503`), and the vector products with dead `m, p` (`.fsi:1508-1523`). The component's `+` and `-` are methods of `trait Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` with one nat (`.fss:2195-2197`), and its products carry one nat `n` (`.fss:2264-2276`). So the api and the component disagree in the number of static parameters, not merely in whether one is constrained. `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs` is `false` with the comment "Not implemented!" (`ExportChecker.scala:645-648`); once it compares, what it compares is a shape mismatch that default-0 at call sites does not touch. The interpreter never runs the export check, which is why the mismatch has lived since 2008.

Why default-0 is the wrong side. A nat left unconstrained by inference and then used as a value in the body (`n.asZZ32`, the spec's "any context a variable of type N32 can appear", `trait-parameters.tex:82-86`) would compute with 0 and no error; the interpreter's analogue, `BottomType` for an unbound parameter (`EvaluatorBase.java:238-240`), errors at first use. The safe rule is the interpreter's: an unsolved nat is an error when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing when it reaches nothing. Whether the six api lines are then edited (a sealed-tree library edit) or the export checker is taught to tolerate a dead parameter is decision E.

## 2. The seven questions, answered by finding

**Q1, finish or redesign.** It finishes the specification's shape: the sized family `Array k[T, 0, n0, …]` over a generic array (`aggregate.tex:130-136`), both factories (`arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`), a linear store under a structure (`:18-22`, `future.tex:42`), sizes in types (`nutshell.tex:85-86`), and the checker doing what the interpreter's `unifyStaticArg` does (`IntNat.java:127-147`). It departs in six places: the storing objects are rewritten, not copied (finding 5, unnamed); the run-time-sized factory's dynamic half, that an `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` is a `Vector` underneath, is dropped (§6d, named as "the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce", but its consequence for the model is not, finding 1); natives in place of the team's generated-code unboxing (finding 4, half named); store selection by run-time tag, our roadmap's A2, in place of the team's `Unbox`/expando direction (finding 2, unnamed); a third library text in the compiler world in place of the spec's Core/Standard split and the ruling's "the standard library" (finding 3, unnamed); and the compiler world's own precedent, the unsized rank-polymorphic `ZZ32Vector`, set aside (§4b, named).

**Q2, the defaults.** Finding 2 (store selection: refuted by probe, alternatives all `.java`, precedent points the other way), finding 4 (loops: measured to buy nothing on the model's shapes, no precedent), finding 7 (unconstrained nats: unsafe side, and the real problem is an api/component mismatch). The smaller defaults: the nat also as a run-time field is right and forced (finding 5); the run-time-sized factory returning the unsized `Array` is what breaks the model (finding 1); one shadow session before the checker edit is right and should widen to five probes (§7 below). Which are Pavol's: all three large ones and the run-time-size one; the shadow session is the worker's.

**Q3, the nat plan.** The Scala side is consistent with itself: `staticInstantiation` already substitutes `IntRef` (`STypesUtil.scala:670`), `staticArgsMatchStaticParams` already accepts an `IntArg` for `KindNat` (`:742-747, 767-772`), self-types are built with `IntArg(IntRef)` for nat kinds (`:338-339, 352-353`), and the equality hole is one line (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:332`). Unsound or unproven: the crash is in Java replacer composition (finding 6); "no arithmetic" refuses three library objects (finding 5); the export checker meets an arity mismatch (finding 7); nothing in the plan or the design touches code generation or the runtime for a nat argument, which the first sized object needs (finding 6). Smallest rung that proves or refutes it: the shadow session with `NatInfer1`, `NatObject1`, `NatValue1`, `XXXNatMismatch1` as the design lists them, plus `NatExtends1` (`object V[\nat n\]() extends S[\n\] end` instantiated as `V[\3\]()`, through code generation and a run) and `NatStore1` (a generic factory returning a monomorphic object, the probe `p1_monostore.fss` as it stands). Dead ends: the `TypeArg`/`IntArg` confusion pervasive in the Java front end; a nat needing a runtime RTTI kind; the checker refusing the library's own storing objects with no arithmetic rule the spec permits.

**Q4, `double[]` under the generic trait.** Stamping cannot produce a `[D` field; the design's probe 1 settles that and the map already said it (`map/README.md:43`). The `ZZ32Vector` precedent proves that a hand-written class can implement a trait's `DefaultTraitMethods`, be a `NamingCzar` special type, and reach Java natives through `import java`, and `FZZ32` proves it under instantiated generic supertraits (finding 9). It does not prove unboxed traffic (probe 2, and `KDotStore`), per-instantiation representation, or anything about nats. The route the design proposes for selecting the store is refused by the checker (finding 2); the route that could give unboxed storage per element type under one generic trait is the loader/code-generator one, which `PLAN.md` step 5 says to probe first and which the design dismissed unprobed.

**Q5, the two preludes.** The compiler world, said in §4c and §7's last paragraph, and no more than said: what it costs (a second algebra, ~1,200 lines of array text, two library texts from then on, the interpreter's copy never checked) and what it forecloses (the library route, a reserved fork) are absent (finding 3).

**Q6, the 26 operations and the three kernels.** As written, none is reachable from the model's text and none of the kernels compiles, for the reason of finding 1; the first failure is `FlatArrays.fss:62`, the second `MicroGptFlat.fss:27`. On values that are statically sized (literal sizes, `vector[\RR64,16\]()`), the design serves: the 14 elementwise maps (declared over `Array[\RR64,I\]`, bodies boxed per element under the question-3 default), the library's products and `Diag`, `transpose` of a `Matrix`. It cannot serve as written: `view`, `row`, `row3`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane` (run-time shapes through `reflect`), `rows` in all four shapes (takes `Matrix`, returns `Array`, so one `rows` cannot feed the next), `gather`, `pick`, `onehot` where the argument is a view's result, and the batched product on `heads`' results. The kernels: `kdot` and `kmat` need `vec`/`mat` to return sized types or `DOT`/juxtaposition to be declared over `Array`; `krows` needs both and `rows`.

**Q7, order and stop.** The first gated rung should not be the checker rung until a shadow rung with no gate has answered five questions (§7 below); the checker rung is right as the first gated rung only if the shadow says the crash is in Scala. The stop conditions are in §7.

## 3. Decisions that are Pavol's

Each as what we do, what it changes, the alternatives, and a labelled default that can be accepted without reading the argument; the argument is in §1.

### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits

What we do: choose the mechanism by which `Vector[\RR64,16\]` gets a `double[]` store while `Vector[\T,16\]` for other `T` gets a boxed one.

What it changes: which `.java` rung the array work needs first, and whether the library's generic factories keep their text.

Alternatives. (A1) The design's default, a factory selecting by run-time type tag under one generic storing object: refused by the checker (finding 2); to keep it, a code-generator special case for the factory, a `.java` rung with no team precedent. (A2) The team's direction: the code generator and loader give a stamped `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,n⟧` a `double[]` field, `Unbox.java` case 1 plus the expando stub; the library's text stays as it is; the largest change, in the loader and `CodeGen`, and `PLAN.md` step 5's own first probe. (A3) Monomorphic storing objects per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]`) beside the generic boxed one, with a monomorphic factory name per element type in the manner of `array1`/`vector` (`.fss:2251`); typed cleanly, no code-generator change, but the model then names `rr64vector`, not `vector`, and the generic `Vector[\T,s0\]` is boxed for every `T` including `RR64` unless the user calls the right factory.

Default: probe A2 first (one shadow experiment, `next-climb.md` §3b's first item), because it is the team's breadcrumb and `PLAN.md`'s order; A3 is the fallback that needs no `.java`; A1 is closed by the probe unless Pavol wants the special case.

### Decision B. Where loops run unboxed

What we do: choose between Java natives per whole-array operation and unboxing `RR64` by static type in generated code.

What it changes: whether the ruling "it cannot be boxed" holds for the model (views, lambdas, `rows`) or only for whole-array operations on stores; and the size of the code-generator work.

Alternatives. (B1) Natives first, the design's default: measured at 8.9×/6.6× primitive on the model's shapes (finding 4), the same as boxed storage; helps `p DOT p` and Adam only; no precedent. (B2) Unboxing by static type first (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1): `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` wherever the checker's type is `RR64`; the library's own Fortress loops (`fill`, `map`, `Vector.dot`) become unboxed without natives; every rung `.java` under the full gate; the team's precedent. (B3) Both, in the order B2 for element access and arithmetic, natives only where a whole-array kernel beats the JIT (a measured residue, not a default).

Default: B2, because it is the only alternative under which the ruling is true of the model, and the kernel measurement in the array rung is then `kdot` in Fortress against `KDotPrim`, not against a native.

### Decision C. Which library the array layer and the model's operations go into

What we do: choose between growing the compiler world (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`) with a copy of the array layer and the algebra above `Number`, and making the interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary`) the prelude the compiler checks.

What it changes: whether the standard library exists once or twice from here on; whether yesterday's commit to `FortressLibrary.fss` and this design's rungs land in the same file; the 92 tower errors and 108 native bindings of the library route (FACTS) against the second copy of about 1,200 lines plus the algebra.

Alternatives. (C1) The compiler world, the design's default. (C2) The library route, `PLAN.md`'s reserved fork: the interpreter's library becomes the checked prelude; the 92 errors are classified first (`next-climb.md` §3b's last item, "one probe"). (C3) One text, two bindings: the array layer and algebra written once in `Library/` in Fortress, with the native bindings the only per-world file (`NativeArray.fss` with `builtinPrimitive` for the interpreter, a compiler-world twin with `import java`); whether the two worlds can share a prelude file is unprobed.

Default: none can be labelled; this is the reserved fork and it is Pavol's. The cheapest fact before deciding is the classification of the 92 errors.

### Decision D. The model's static types

What we do: decide how `MicroGptFlat.fss` and `FlatArrays.fss` are typed for a static checker, given that today their values are statically unsized and their operations are declared on sized types (finding 1).

What it changes: the model's text, or the vocabulary's declarations, or the compile path.

Alternatives. (D1) The model carries sizes in its types as the specification intends (`makeVector`, `trait-parameters.tex:94-97`): `step` and its helpers become generic in `nat` parameters, the hyperparameters become static arguments, and every `Array[\RR64,…\]` in the model becomes a `Vector`/`Matrix`/`Array3` with nats; the ruling of `POSITIONS.md:38` requires the diff to be shown before it is built. (D2) The vocabulary is declared over the unsized `Array[\RR64,I\]` and the products the model uses (`DOT`, juxtaposition, `rows`, `gather`, `diag`) are added over `Array` beside the library's sized ones; the model's text is unchanged; the sized products and the shape check are then not what the model exercises, which is the sidestep the second ruling refuses. (D3) A compile-path `reflect`: a native that asks the loader for `N⟦n⟧` by name at run time, which the team's own comment asks for ("we ought to build it in", `NatReflect.fss:39`); it keeps the model's dynamic dispatch but does not make the static types sized, so it does not by itself pass the checker; it is what D1 needs for the run-time-sized parameter vector.

Default: D1 with D3, because both rulings are honoured only there; D2 is the honest alternative if the model's text is to stay byte-identical. The first thing to show Pavol is the D1 diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, not a rung.

### Decision E. The six api declarations with dead nats

What we do: decide what the checker does with `nat m` and `nat p` in `.fsi:1496-1523`, which the component does not have.

What it changes: whether the checker rung touches `Library/` (six api lines) and what an unsolved nat means anywhere.

Alternatives. (E1) Default to 0, the design's: unsafe when the parameter is later used as a value (finding 7), and blind to the api/component shape mismatch. (E2) Unsolved is an error when the nat reaches a type, a name or a value, nothing otherwise (the interpreter's `BottomType` rule); the six declarations pass because their dead parameters reach nothing; the export checker compares by name and reports the extra parameter. (E3) Delete the dead parameters from the api, a sealed-tree library edit flagged at commit, and the export checker then agrees.

Default: E2 in the checker, E3 as the library edit shown to Pavol as a six-line diff; not E1.

### Decision F. What the first gated rung is, and what stops the climb

What we do: run a shadow rung with no gate before the checker rung, answering: where the `VarType`/`IntExpr` crash comes from; what the export checker reports on the six declarations; whether a generic object with a nat argument in `extends` can be stamped and run (`NatExtends1`); whether the store can be selected under the generic factory in any typed way (`NatStore1`, decision A); and whether the loader can be made to select a representation (decision A2). Then the checker rung.

Stop conditions to adopt, each returning to Pavol with the capture: the crash's fix is in a Java front-end class, so the plan's "no Java" and its size are void; a nat argument needs a new RTTI kind in `runtimeSystem/`; the checker refuses every typed route to the store (A1 and A3 both fail); the model cannot be typed without a diff to its lines (decision D not taken); the kernel compiled over the store lands at the `KDotStore` number rather than the `KDotPrim` number, which means the traffic is still boxed.

## 4. Verdict

Unsound as written. The two rulings stand and the shape the design draws from them, sized traits over a native linear store with the checker doing what `unifyStaticArg` does, is the specification's own shape and has the team's breadcrumbs behind it (`future.tex:42`, `arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`, `MethodMapping.tex:142`). But three load-bearing claims fail: the plan cannot compile the program it is measured by, because it keeps the model's unsized static types and the checker resolves statically (finding 1); its default mechanism for putting `double[]` under the generic trait is refused by the checker, and the branch it dismissed is the team's (finding 2); and it closes the second reserved fork in one line (finding 3). It becomes sound only under conditions Pavol sets: decision D taken and its diff shown; decision A taken after the loader probe `PLAN.md` step 5 already orders; decision C taken as the fork it is; decision B taken with the `KDotStore` measurement in view; and the shadow rung and stop conditions of decision F adopted before the first gated rung.

## The library's arrays and algebra

- `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` are the only sized array traits; `Array3[\T, nat b0, nat s0, …\]` carries no algebraic trait (row 292; `FortressLibrary.fsi:1460, 1578, 1652`).
- `Vector` and `Matrix` inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` from `AdditiveGroup`, nothing else; `×` reaches no array by design because juxtaposition is the inner product and the array traits exclude `AnyMultiplicativeRing` (rows 64, 109, 293); a carrier that extends the ring is accepted unchecked, changes juxtaposition to elementwise and breaks `+` (vocabulary review v02, v02b).
- The library's products are declared with shared `nat`s (`Matrix[\T,n,m\]` × `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1516`); C4's own products were not, which is habit; the focused base's `FlatArrays2` states them (twelve declarations including the per-rank elementwise `×` and `/`, 25 of 29 nats agreeing; 39 declarations), and a wrong-shape call is refused at dispatch, uncatchable for an overloaded name (row 83), as a unification error naming the nat for an unoverloaded one (`apl/mg/checks/mismatch_probe.out`).
- Two declarations of one name differing only in the element type, or a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one, are refused at load ("at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types"; `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.0`, `elemwise_nat_probe.out.0`); two apis' overloads of one name are checked as one family, so two vocabularies cannot stand in one component (`diag_fwd_two_vocabularies_rejected.out.0`).
- The shipped `RR64` does not satisfy the specification's algebraic bound `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (vocabulary review, probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); `T extends Number` is the bound that works for every element type and rank (row 295).
- The library's scalar-extension block for `+ - MIN MAX` over arrays is generic since `02d09a39f` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4511-4521`, `.fsi:2550-2560`); no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel exists in the library (vocabulary review, section A).
- An array is a trait with `get`/`put`; a view is an object implementing it over other storage, the language's own idiom; the library's row slice `m[i,:]` costs 5× a six-line user view; a diagonal as a `Matrix` view costs 13-54× the operator (vocabulary review v20, v07).
- The element type is `Number` only for `Vector`/`Matrix` (row 24); irrelevant to numeric microGPT, decisive for Run B's autodiff value and for APL characters.
